name: Phosphorus
occurrence: Never found free; combined in phosphate rock (apatite) and in every living cell's DNA and ATP.
biologicalRelevance: A structural component of DNA's backbone and of ATP, the molecule your cells use to store and transfer chemical energy — no phosphorus, no energy metabolism.
notableCharacteristics: White phosphorus glows faintly in the dark (chemiluminescence, the origin of the word 'phosphorescence') and ignites spontaneously in air, so it's stored underwater.
whyHere: Five valence electrons like nitrogen above it, but a much larger atomic size means weaker pi-bonding, so phosphorus favours single-bonded, more complex structures like P₄ tetrahedra instead of a simple diatomic gas.
didYouKnow: Hennig Brand discovered phosphorus in 1669 by boiling down thousands of litres of urine looking for gold — instead he isolated a glowing white waxy solid.
genZNote: Discovered in urine, now it's in your DNA and your matchsticks. A genuine glow-up story.
